## A better cup. A more curious mind.

You pour water over leaves. A few minutes later, you have something fragrant, warming, and surprisingly complicated. Why does the same tea taste gentle one morning and bitter the next? What does a name on the packet actually tell you? And how much of a tea headline should you believe?

Start with the cup in front of you. Follow your curiosity from there.

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-4}

[Start with tea basics →](tea-basics.qmd)
:::
::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-4}

Try the same leaves with two steeping times. Discover what changes in the water—and what taste alone cannot tell you.

[Try the brewing lesson →](modules/module-01/03-brewing.qmd)

## One small experiment to begin

Next time you make tea, notice three things before reaching for a verdict: **what you smell, what you taste, and how your mouth feels afterwards**. “I don't like this tea” is a starting point. “I like the aroma, but the finish is too drying” gives you something to work with.

The [brewing lesson](modules/module-01/03-brewing.qmd#try-it-two-cups-one-change) turns that observation into a simple comparison. If your mug needs rescuing right now, go straight to [Kitchen troubleshoot](tea-troubleshoot.qmd).

## Follow the leaf beyond the kettle

Tea Companion has **five chapters and twenty lessons**. Read them in order for a journey from leaf to everyday life, or begin with a question that interests you.

| Your question | Where it leads |
| --- | --- |
| How can one plant become such different teas? | [**1 · The Chemical Core**](modules/module-01/index.qmd): plants, processing, brewing, and compounds |
| What happens after I drink it? | [**2 · Body, Brain & Mood**](modules/module-02/index.qmd): brain signaling, brain waves, stress hormones, and body signals |
| How did a drink become part of trade and daily culture? | [**3 · History & Culture**](modules/module-03/index.qmd): trade, monastic traditions, plantations, and regional customs |
| How much does the setting shape the experience? | [**4 · Context & Ritual Psychology**](modules/module-04/index.qmd): warmth, ritual, expectations, and labels |
| Can a drink change a decision—and how would we know? | [**5 · Decisions & Choices**](modules/module-05/index.qmd): quick judgments, risk, patience, trust, and study design |

[Browse all twenty lessons →](modules/index.qmd)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: the full reading journey"}
Begin with the leaf: where tea comes from, how processing changes it, what brewing extracts, and the compounds you will meet again. Then move into the body and the studies used to investigate brain activity, mood, stress, and body signals.

The view widens in the history chapter, from trade to monastic traditions, plantations, and regional customs. The final chapters ask how warmth, ritual, expectations, and social settings enter the experience—and how researchers investigate judgments, risk, patience, and trust. These are questions to explore, not promises that a cup will produce a particular effect.

Each chapter has four lessons:

1. **[The Chemical Core](modules/module-01/index.qmd):** Plants · Processing · Brewing · Compounds.
2. **[Body, Brain & Mood](modules/module-02/index.qmd):** Brain action · Brain waves · Stress hormones · Body signals.
3. **[History & Culture](modules/module-03/index.qmd):** Trade history · Monastic path · Plantation aftershock · Regional scripts.
4. **[Context & Ritual Psychology](modules/module-04/index.qmd):** Warmth & trust · Ritual & stress · Expectation & labels · Context dials map.
5. **[Decisions & Choices](modules/module-05/index.qmd):** Dual-process · Risk & waiting · Trust games · Study protocols.

Read in sequence, or use [Linkages](linkages.qmd) to follow connections between chapters. Tea basics and the label guide can be read before Chapter 1 or alongside it.
:::

## Keep these beside your cup

- **Something tastes wrong?** [Kitchen troubleshoot](tea-troubleshoot.qmd) helps you choose one brewing adjustment.
- **A headline sounds too good?** [Reading a tea study](tea-reading-studies.qmd) offers five questions to ask about the evidence.
- **Looking for quantities?** [Cup reference](cup-reference.qmd) gathers estimates for a 250 mL mug. Treat them as orientation, not a measurement of your particular brew.
- **Lost in terminology?** The [Glossary](glossary.qmd) gives short definitions; [Linkages](linkages.qmd) connects ideas across chapters.

## Read a little, or go deeper

You do not need a chemistry background or special teaware. Begin with an observation, follow the explanation, and use the optional **More detail** foldouts when you want to look closer. Footnotes lead to sources, and the [Bibliography](bibliography.qmd) brings the references together.

As you read, keep three questions separate: **What changed in the cup? What did a study measure? What did I personally notice?** A finding about extracted compounds does not, by itself, establish an effect on mood or decisions. Learning to make those distinctions is part of the pleasure of understanding tea.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: using sources and reference pages"}
Click a footnote number to jump to its source; use the return arrow to come back. In browsers that support it, hovering can also show a preview. Expand a **More detail** box to read its tables or explanation without leaving the lesson.

When a number appears, check the preparation it describes. Tea, leaf amount, cup size, and steeping conditions can differ. The [Cup reference](cup-reference.qmd) gathers everyday estimates for a 250 mL cup; the [Bibliography](bibliography.qmd) helps you find the papers behind the claims. The [Glossary](glossary.qmd) is there for a quick definition.
:::

The companion is also available in [香港繁體中文](zh-hant-hk/index.qmd) and [简体中文](zh-hans/index.qmd).

You tip hot water over a handful of leaves. Steam rises. The water darkens—maybe green-gold, maybe deep amber—and a smell fills the room that is somehow both sharp and soft. Twenty minutes later you are a little more awake. Sometimes you also feel a little calmer. Coffee can wake you up too. So why does *tea* so often feel like a different kind of alertness?

That question is the door into this site.

This site is a **story-shaped journey** through tea. It moves from the leaves, to the body and mood, through history and warmth, and on to everyday decisions. Each lesson aims to stay interesting, and short enough to feel like a story.

**Footnotes** work in both directions: the number jumps to the source, and the caret jumps back. Hover often shows a popup. Denser tables and side-stories sit in collapsed **"More detail…"** foldouts. The [Bibliography](bibliography.qmd) is the master map.

## What this journey is about

Think of five chapters that follow one continuous thread. Each chapter has **four lessons**.

First you meet the **leaf**: where tea comes from, why green and black look so different, what brewing pulls into the mug, and three headline compounds. Then you follow those compounds **into the body**, through brain signaling, brain-wave patterns, stress hormones, and quiet body signals. Next you zoom out. Tea remade **trade balances**, became a monastic focus aid, and even a warm mug in the hand shows up in experiments on trust. A short brewing break can also act as a practical stress reset. Finally you ask the decision question. Do drinks **nudge** how fast we answer, how much risk we take, how much we care about tomorrow, and how trusting we are in a first move?

You can start anywhere. If you read in order, each lesson hands you a reason to open the next.

## How to travel with this site

When a number appears—say "about 30–50 mg caffeine"—treat it as a **typical range**, not a promise about your exact mug. Brands, leaves, and steep times differ. The [Cup reference](cup-reference.qmd) is the quick table for a common 250 mL cup.

If you are new to tea itself, start with **[Tea basics](tea-basics.qmd)** and make a first mug. If a shelf or cafe name is still foggy, open **[Tea labels](tea-labels.qmd)** before Chapter 1, or alongside it.

When a technical word appears, we define it in the story the first time. The [Glossary](glossary.qmd) is there when you want a one-line reminder, with links into the right chapter hub.

When you wonder how a brewing fact connects to mood, or how a warm mug connects to a trust game, open [Linkages](linkages.qmd). Those eleven bridges sew the chapters together.

When you want the paper behind a name-and-year, or the note behind a footnote marker on a lesson page, click the footnote or open the [Bibliography](bibliography.qmd).

Ready? Pour an imaginary cup. Start with [Tea basics](tea-basics.qmd) for a first mug. Open [Tea labels](tea-labels.qmd) if a box or menu name is still foggy. Open [Kitchen troubleshoot](tea-troubleshoot.qmd) if the mug already went wrong. Read [Reading a tea study](tea-reading-studies.qmd) before you trust a headline. Then open [Chapter 1: The Chemical Core](modules/module-01/index.qmd), or skim the [roadmap](modules/index.qmd) first.
